A set of catgories constitutes an

if they collectively define the various modes of existence for a collection of related things. For example, we may want to distinguish between things that are real or imaginary, concrete or abstract, mental or material, etc.
The need for such an ontology follows from the fact that
existing vocabularies reflect different levels of description
, ranging from specific and concrete actions to more general ones. Existing classificaiton by
are useful but orthogonal to the task of differentiating between actions that are general and specific.
In addition, current vocabularies, taken as whole, do not compose a complete set of terms to fully describe the process of data exploration and visualization.

The following ontology is proposed as a simple partitioning of the space of actions in order to facilitate the process of converting actions into artifacts for visualization, e.g. dashboards and infographics.
The ontology presented here is based on summarizing a collection of vocabulary terms proposed by students in UVA’s DS 2023 course, Communicating with Data.
Based on a review of a
, we propose the following four categories:
: Maps to one or a few specific function calls; a single, unambiguous operation.
: Composed of multiple atomic operations; requires a sequence of steps.
: Describes an intent or design principle; no direct translation to a tool operation.
: Describes the analyst’s role or process; not a data or visual operation at all.

(marked in their rows): Declare, Select, Retrieve Value (also from Amar et al. 2005), Transform (Statistical), Layer, Map (visual), and Draw. Eleven further terms were added by editorial assessment: Impute, Interpolate (data-level), Sample, Encode, Bin, Reduce (Data Preparation); Smooth, Resample, Decompose (Temporal Analysis); Style, Legend (Visual Encoding).
Several recurring coherence issues appear across categories:
: Trace / Track; Correlate / Co-vary / Relate; Show Proportion / Apportion / Compose; Estimate / Approximate; Isolate / Trim / Eliminate all cover essentially the same ground.
: Transform, Distribute, Display, Customize, and Assign are placeholders for entire categories, not discrete operations.
: Characterize Distribution and Find Anomalies feel atomic in intent but require multiple function calls in practice.
